content: 1. A study conducted in 2001 highlighted the health risks faced by children living in environments contaminated with lead. 2. Wright et al. (2003) investigated the relationship between iron deficiency and blood lead levels in children attending an urban primary care clinic. Their longitudinal analysis, published in The Journal of Pediatrics, revealed a significant association between iron deficiency and elevated lead levels. 3. Khan et al. Their findings, published in the World Journal of Pediatrics, demonstrated a synergistic effect, where iron deficiency exacerbated lead absorption. 4. Gulson et al. (1997) reported that pregnancy increases the mobilization of lead stored in the maternal skeleton. 5. Janakiraman et al. (2003) conducted a randomized crossover trial to assess the impact of calcium supplementation on bone resorption during pregnancy. Their findings, published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine, suggested that calcium supplementation could reduce bone mobilization. 6. Avendaño-Badillo et al. (2009) demonstrated that high dietary calcium intake decreases bone mobilization during pregnancy. This study, published in Salud Pública de México, highlighted the protective role of calcium in reducing lead release from bones. 7. Kwong et al. (2004) reviewed the interactions between iron deficiency and lead poisoning, focusing on epidemiology and pathogenesis. Their work, published in Science of the Total Environment, provided insights into the mechanisms by which iron deficiency increases lead absorption. 8. Ahamed and Siddiqui (2007) examined the interplay between environmental lead toxicity and nutritional factors. Their study, published in Clinical Nutrition, emphasized the importance of adequate nutrition in mitigating lead toxicity. 9. Ross et al. (2011) published dietary reference intakes for calcium and vitamin D through the National Academies Press. 10. Gurer and Ercal (2000) investigated the potential benefits of antioxidants in treating lead poisoning. 11. Simon and Hudes (1999) explored the relationship between ascorbic acid (vitamin C) and blood lead levels. Their study, published in JAMA, found that higher ascorbic acid levels were associated with lower blood lead concentrations. 12. Haryanto and Sutrisna (2013) evaluated the effect of calcium supplementation on blood lead levels in Indonesian schoolchildren. Their study, published in the International Journal of Scientific Research, demonstrated a reduction in blood lead levels with calcium supplementation. 13. Zhao et al. (1998) conducted a double-blind randomized clinical trial to assess the therapeutic effectiveness of calcium supplementation in children with moderate lead poisoning. Their findings, published in the Chinese Journal of Pediatrics, supported the use of calcium in reducing lead levels. 14. Sofyani and Lelo (2016) emphasized the role of calcium supplementation in preventing lead poisoning in children. Their study, published in Advances in Health Science Research, highlighted the importance of dietary interventions in lead-exposed populations. 15. Markowitz et al. (2004) conducted a randomized trial to evaluate the efficacy of calcium supplementation in treating childhood lead poisoning. Their findings, published in Pediatrics, demonstrated a significant reduction in blood lead levels with calcium supplementation. 16. Allen et al. (2011) published guidelines on food fortification with micronutrients through the World Health Organization (WHO). These guidelines aim to address nutritional deficiencies and reduce lead absorption in vulnerable populations. 17. Zimmermann et al. (2006) demonstrated that iron fortification reduced blood lead levels in children in Bangalore, India. Their study, published in Pediatrics, highlighted the role of iron in mitigating lead toxicity. 18. Rosado et al. (2006) conducted a randomized placebo-controlled trial to assess the impact of iron and zinc supplementation on blood lead concentrations in children. Their findings, published in the Journal of Nutrition, indicated no significant reduction in lead levels. 19. WHO (2011) released guidelines on daily iron supplementation for infants and children to address iron deficiency and reduce lead absorption. 20. Bouhouch et al. (2016) evaluated the effects of iron-fortified wheat-flour biscuits on blood lead levels, iron status, and cognition in children. Their study, published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, demonstrated improvements in iron status and cognitive outcomes. 21. Kordas et al. (2005) found that iron and zinc supplementation did not improve behavior ratings in lead-exposed Mexican schoolchildren. Their study, published in The Journal of Pediatrics, highlighted the complexity of addressing lead toxicity. 22. Rico et al. (2006) assessed the efficacy of iron and zinc supplementation on cognitive performance in lead-exposed Mexican schoolchildren. Their findings, published in Pediatrics, indicated no significant improvement in cognitive outcomes. 23. Khan and Tisman (2010) reported on cases of pica associated with iron deficiency. Their study, published in the Journal of Medical Case Reports, emphasized the need for addressing nutritional deficiencies in lead-exposed populations. 24. WHO (2019) published the 7th edition of the Model List of Essential Medicines for Children, which includes recommendations for managing lead poisoning. 25. Ettinger et al. (2009) conducted a randomized placebo-controlled trial to evaluate the effect of calcium supplementation on blood lead levels during pregnancy. Their findings, published in Environmental Health Perspectives, demonstrated a reduction in maternal blood lead levels. 26. Hofmeyr et al. (2018) reviewed the role of calcium supplementation during pregnancy in preventing hypertensive disorders. Their systematic review, published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, highlighted the benefits of calcium in maternal health. 27. Hernandez-Avila et al. (2003) demonstrated that dietary calcium supplements lowered blood lead levels in lactating women. Their study, published in Epidemiology, emphasized the importance of calcium in reducing lead transfer to breast milk. 28. Ettinger et al. (2006) investigated the influence of maternal bone lead burden and calcium intake on lead levels in breast milk. Their findings, published in the American Journal of Epidemiology, highlighted the protective role of calcium during lactation. 29. Downie et al. (2016) conducted a systematic review to identify antenatal care processes and outcomes important to pregnant women. Their findings, published in the British Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology, emphasized the need for patient-centered care. 30. WHO (2021) released updated recommendations on antenatal care, including nutritional interventions such as vitamin D supplementation during pregnancy, to improve maternal and fetal outcomes.
